failures: M8 defect found while making the M9 regression gate run: app/api/ws.py EVENT_NAMES had no entry for the runtime's 'done' and 'error' events, so every run end and every failure reached WebSocket clients as 'agent_update' and the documented names were unreachable. The test that covered it (test_console_api.py::test_ws_run_streams_documented_events) waited forever for a frame that could not arrive, which is why the backend suite hung for minutes instead of failing. Mapping added and guarded by tests in tests/test_ws.py.

Known parser limitations recorded as known_gap in backend/evaluation/parser_golden.jsonl (not fixed in M9, which is an evaluation milestone): a truncated second call after a complete one is dropped without any issue; a call quoted as an example in prose is executed like a real one; identical calls are returned twice.
decisions: M1 drives the browser through a selector-driven WebChatProvider fed by JSON provider profiles; site detail never lives in provider or (future) agent code.
The browser is always headed: BrowserDriver(headless=True) raises BrowserConfigError, and no stealth/fingerprint/automation-evasion launch flags are used.
Login is manual by design: recover_session only re-opens the page and waits for a human to sign in; no credential, captcha or risk-control automation exists.

Completion detection is multi-signal (stop control gone + text unchanged for stable_polls polls + non-empty text) with a mandatory timeout fallback that returns partial text, timed_out=True and a persisted timeline.
Reply capture priority is network/SSE > copy button > DOM. Network bodies are only read for responses whose request already finished, so an open stream can never block capture.

Verified offline against a shipped fixture chat page (backend/fixtures/chat_site) that streams SSE, exposes a stop control and can show a login wall; the shipped mock profile is marked verified, while example-web-llm.json is an explicitly UNVERIFIED template - no real web LLM site was driven in this session.
Artifacts are written per run to runs/<timestamp>-<profile>/ (screenshot, DOM html+text, timeline, reply, network log); runs/ and .browser-profile/ are gitignored.
playwright is pinned to 1.62.0 in the repo venv so it reuses the Chromium build already installed at C:\Users\LIN\AppData\Local\ms-playwright (chromium-1234).
M1 delivered no frontend or API changes: the browser layer is not yet reachable from the web console (no Tool/AgentLoop may call it until later milestones).

Subagent delegation was broken in this environment: children inherit the parent agent's create-time route (agent.options), not its live model route, so after a mid-session default-model switch every delegation hit the stale opencode-go provider and failed with 400 MissingSessionID (missing x-opencode-session). Root cause proven from the child session logs and fixed by pinning config.agentOptions (provider commandcode / model deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash) on the tool-subagent and tool-subagent-fork rows of the liangshen agent preset; the pin needs a DSH restart or a new session to mount, and the workflow tool passing an explicit provider/model works as an immediate workaround (verified).

M2 memory entries are typed (MemoryEntry: key/value/namespace/source/sensitive/source_turn/updated_by/timestamps) instead of an opaque list; this supersedes the M0 assertion that memory.json round-trips verbatim, so tests/test_storage.py::test_memory_round_trip now asserts the typed round trip plus defaults.

M2 transcripts are stored as append-only JSONL per session under state/sessions/ (gitignored): a crash can only tear the last line, and the reader skips unparsable lines instead of losing the whole transcript.
M2 external content is untrusted: the ContextBuilder renders tool results/DOM text with an explicit untrusted marker, and MemoryStore rejects secrets before they can be persisted.

Command Code provider: patched the installed 0.9.1 in place (reasoning replay on the CLI transport + selectable reasoning efforts for deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash) because the upstream fix ships in 0.10.5, which requires dsh >= 0.1.2-rc.1 and this machine runs dsh 0.1.1-rc.1. Patch and backup are stored next to the plugin and in ~/.dsh/patches/; it must be re-applied after any plugin update.

M2 context budget is measured in characters, not tokens: there is no tokenizer behind the provider boundary yet. ContextBuilder truncates non-protected sections (head+tail, omitting-size recorded, reference kept) and drops the lowest priority ones; system and task are never dropped.

M2 rotation seeds the new session with a BOUNDED summary (seed_summary_chars, default 1500). Embedding the full summary rebuilt a context as large as the one rotation existed to escape (observed: 8225 -> 8245 chars in a test before the fix).

Rotation only reclaims space when the session is near the budget; the seed is a fixed cost, so rotating a small session can grow the context. should_rotate() is the documented gate and the rotate CLI prints the before/after sizes plus a note instead of hiding it.

M2 REST surface is read-only (/api/sessions, /api/sessions/{id}, /api/messages, /api/context) and no endpoint executes anything; the Tool layer arrives in M3 behind SafetyLayer/Executor. Named after docs/api-protocol.md, keeping /api/project_state and /api/memory.
M2 memory dedupe compares VALUES only: the same key with a different value is a conflict, not a duplicate (the first implementation classified it as duplicate, which silently swallowed the conflict).

M2 skips the project_state context section entirely when the state holds nothing factual, so an unstarted project does not push placeholder lines into every turn (docs/state-context.md forbids injecting everything by default).
M3 tool arguments are strict (extra='forbid'): an invented parameter is a schema violation, because silently dropping it would hide that the model misunderstood the tool.

M3 does not expose tools over REST: with no SafetyLayer yet, an HTTP entry point to run_shell/write_file would be a hole. Manual use goes through app.tools.cli, which uses the same Executor and bypasses nothing.

M3 parser reports no_tool_call (not invalid_json) when the output contains no JSON structure at all, but keeps a specific issue code when a real structure failed to parse; otherwise the model hunts a syntax error that does not exist.
M3 Executor logs replayed idempotent calls too: a replay is still a call that happened, and omitting it would make the audit log under-report (found by a test).
M3 apply_patch writes nothing unless every hunk matches exactly once, so a partially applied patch can never leave a file half-modified.

M4 replaces the M3 seam with a real SafetyLayer. The documented order is ToolCall -> Validation -> SafetyLayer -> Confirmation; validation therefore runs BEFORE the assessment, so a wrongly typed argument is a schema error rather than a safety error.

There is no unchecked Executor: omitting the safety argument makes the Executor build a layer scoped to its working directory. A test asserts the attribute is never None and that an explicit spy layer observes every execution.

M4 file scope is enforced on the RESOLVED path so a symlink cannot step outside the project, extra roots must be configured explicitly, and sensitive names (.env, id_rsa, key suffixes, .ssh/.aws/.gnupg) are refused even inside the project.

M4 shell grading is deny-by-default: an unrecognised verb is HIGH, never LOW; every segment of a chained command is graded; subcommands are graded too (git status is LOW, git push is HIGH); a denied command is always reported HIGH regardless of its verb.

M4 denies rather than confirms the operations no human answer should authorise: destructive patterns (rm -rf /, dd of=/dev/..., curl|bash, git push --force), commands naming a sensitive file, and commands touching a path outside the project. A confirmation cannot override a deny.

M4 prompt-injection defence is two-part: instruction-like content in untrusted text is flagged and travels with the result (whose text is never rewritten), and check_instruction_source() refuses to parse tool/file/web/shell/document output as instructions, so only model and user output can issue a tool call.
M4 session grants are keyed by the exact command (for run_shell) or the exact arguments, so 本会话允许 never widens into a blanket shell grant; the tests pin that a grant does not cover another command.

M4 confirmation is rendered in the terminal (app.safety.cli confirm) with the four required facts and the three choices. The web console is NOT wired yet: that needs the confirm_request event from docs/api-protocol.md, which belongs with the API-protocol work rather than the safety layer.
M5 is a single-agent loop only; docs/runtime-agents.md requires the single loop to be solid before multi-agent orchestration, and session/browser/login recovery belongs to M6.

The loop is model-agnostic behind a ModelClient protocol. BrowserModel adapts the M1 provider (so a web page is the real model end); ScriptedModel and CallableModel make the loop deterministic in tests, and the acceptance test uses a CallableModel whose decision depends on the tool results in the prompt — that is what proves 根据结果继续.

Tool results are recorded in the session transcript with the 'tool' role. The context only carries the previous step's results, so without this the model would lose what earlier tools returned; found while writing the acceptance test.

Confirmation is answered BEFORE the execution attempts, so a tool retry applies to the real run rather than to a refusal (found by a test: a shell timeout was never retried because the refusal consumed the retry loop).
Loop detection matches repeating cycles up to 4 steps long, not just consecutive identical calls, so an A,B,A,B pattern is caught (found by a test).
A tool failure is retried only when the Executor marks it retryable; ToolExecutionError now takes an explicit retryable flag and the shell timeout sets it, while a missing file stays non-retryable.

Plain prose is a completion signal, not a parse failure: parse retries apply only when nothing usable was parsed, and a partial parse (one good call plus one unknown tool) keeps the good call instead of retrying it away.
The idempotency cache is invalidated by any non-read-only call: a replayed read was showing the agent file content from before a write (found by the acceptance test).

The M1 provider's network capture is scoped to the current exchange via a cursor; before this, a second question on the same page captured the first answer's stream as well (found by the M5 browser integration test).
Only model and user output may be parsed as instructions; the loop calls the safety instruction-source guard on every reply.

M6 context thresholds are ratios of the builder budget (soft 0.7, hard 0.9), so the policy follows whatever budget M2 is configured with instead of duplicating a character count. The loop evaluates them at every step boundary, which is what makes 'finish the turn first' true by construction.

SessionRecovery verifies the four injections (Project State, Memory, Recent Transcript, current task) instead of assuming them, but treats 'nothing to inject' as satisfied: rotating an empty session is not a failure, and a check that cries wolf gets ignored.
A rotation carries the last N turns verbatim as well as a bounded summary of the older ones, so the task continues with real conversational context rather than only a summary.

BrowserRecovery restarts a dead page and waits for a MANUAL login on expiry, bounded by a restart budget and a login timeout; call() retries once after a successful recovery rather than looping around a page that keeps dying.

BrowserModel now accepts provider_factory. Recovery replaces the page, so a model holding the old provider kept talking to a dead one (found by the M6 browser-crash acceptance test); the factory form is what lets the loop follow the restarted page.

The AgentLoop gained restore_model_state (default True). A real model is stateless, so the stored snapshot is only a hint for a deterministic one; a caller supplying a fresh model (a new --script, or a rebuilt page) sets it False, otherwise the checkpoint silently rewinds the new model past its first reply (found in the CLI acceptance run).

The recovery REST surface is read-only; a reconnecting client re-reads facts rather than the server keeping them in memory. FastAPI's legacy '= Query(gt=...)' form does not validate, so the pressure endpoint uses Annotated and maps an inverted threshold pair to 422 rather than a 500.
M6 did not implement multi-agent orchestration (M7), and did not automate credentials: login recovery only waits for the human, per the project's standing rule.

M7 enforces role boundaries by CAPABILITY: each role gets a registry holding only its allowed tools (ToolRegistry.subset), so a Planner has no write tool registered. A prompt can be ignored; an absent tool cannot be called. An unknown name in an allowlist raises instead of silently widening it.

The roles share one session and one Project State / Memory, per docs/runtime-agents.md ('roles share Project State, Memory, current task, necessary context'). Each role's isolation comes from its system prompt and its tool registry, not from a separate transcript — which also lets the Reviewer see what the Coder actually did.

Verdicts are parsed from a fixed shape; an answer without a verdict is 'unknown', treated as a fix request for the Reviewer and as not-blocked for the SafetyGuard. Assuming approval from unparseable text is how a broken review silently passes.

M7 bounds the collaboration four ways: max_rounds, each role's own max_steps, a wall-clock budget checked before each round, and stall detection (the same verdict AND the same issues twice stops the run). The orchestrator takes an injectable clock so the time bound is provable in a test without waiting.

AgentOrchestrator accepts model_factory so a deployment can route roles to different models (a stronger reviewer), and so tests can script each role separately; a single shared reply queue is unusable for roles that make several model calls per run (found while writing the CLI acceptance).

Role tool calls are written to the same runs/tool-calls.jsonl audit log as single-agent runs (found in the acceptance run: role Executors had no log path, so multi-agent work went unaudited). Confirmations are recorded there too.
The orchestrator collects the roles' events into OrchestrationResult; without them the result showed that a role failed but not why (found by a test).

M8 keeps every execution boundary: the console runs the same AgentLoop/AgentOrchestrator, so the M4 SafetyLayer, the Executor and the audit log apply unchanged; the runtime adds observation, a stop flag and a confirmation channel, not a new execution path.

The runtime serves ONE run at a time (a second start is 409). The event ring, the stop flag and the confirmation queue describe exactly one run, so allowing two would make 'stop' and 'confirm' ambiguous.

An unanswered confirmation expires and is treated as a rejection, so a run can never hang because a browser tab was closed. The default policy is 'ask'; 'auto_once' exists for unattended runs and 'deny' for a locked-down one.

Tool call ids are now unique for the whole run (<run>-<step>-<index>). They were unique only within one parse, and since each step parses a single call every id was 'call-1'; the console pairs tool_call with tool_result by id, so all three cards collapsed into one (found by driving the real UI, not by a unit test).
A confirmation's answer is published as an agent_update, not a tool_result: the old typing produced a result with no call_id, which a console renders as a phantom card.

The WS protocol carries two frame families on one socket (M0 echo plus the documented envelope), and correlation ids (request_id, tool_call_id, agent_id) are TOP-LEVEL as docs/api-protocol.md requires, so a client can key on them without reading the payload.
Frontend types are generated from the backend OpenAPI schema (scripts/gen-api-types.mjs, committed snapshot) so no backend model is maintained twice, per docs/api-protocol.md.

Contract alignment after the frontend reported mismatches: the confirmation policy is ask|auto_once|deny with 'once' accepted as a normalised alias, POST /api/sessions accepts the title as a body or a query parameter, and confirm_request carries request_id in the payload and at the top level.

M9 providers are a registry behind the same ModelClient protocol the loop already used: the browser, an offline scripted replay and an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint are three registrations, and app/agents is untouched (a test asserts the loop module never mentions the registry).

The registry rejects an option name a provider does not declare, but one settings document may still hold every adapter's options: options are filtered by declared name for the ACTIVE adapter, so a typo for the running provider still raises while an inactive adapter's base_url is simply not passed.
A provider option marked secret is never written to the settings document: it is read from the environment (api_key_env) when the model is built, and stripped on save.

Choosing a provider is configuration, not code: deps.build_console_model() resolves adapter/model/options from the settings document, and saving a different provider drops the cached model so the next run uses what the page shows.

The evaluation harness runs the REAL components (parser, SafetyLayer, Executor, AgentLoop, SessionManager) in a throwaway workspace per case; only the model is scripted, and the recovery cases break it on purpose first (fault injection), so 'recovery' is demonstrated rather than assumed.

A case carries its contract, and the harness reports the difference; it never rewrites the expectation to match the implementation. Observed behaviour that is a genuine limitation is recorded in a known_gap field whose expectation still describes today's behaviour, and the regression test asserts that gap is unchanged - so fixing one forces a dataset update in the same change.

Thresholds require 100% of both suites plus coverage of the eight parser categories, the six dimensions and the case counts, so a regression fails the suite instead of quietly lowering a number. A suite that did not run is absent (None) rather than an empty report, because an empty report reads as 'ran and found nothing'.

M9 evaluated the agent, it did not re-implement it: the three parser limitations the golden set exposed are recorded and left to a future change, because fixing M3 parse behaviour is not this milestone's task.

The five M6 acceptance scenarios are covered by real components: program restart (CLI + tests), context threshold (rotation and soft compaction), WebSocket disconnect (snapshot re-sync), browser crash (a real page killed mid-run and restarted), login expiry (a real login wall plus a simulated manual sign-in).
Recovery is bounded everywhere: a restart budget, a login timeout, one retry per call and a bounded parse retry. Nothing retries forever.

docs/runtime-agents.md's four hard constraints are each covered by tests: no Executor bypass (roles hold no tools, and the role registry is the only way in), no direct shared-state writes (only the two tools change state), no infinite loop (round/step/time bounds), no infinite conversation (stall detection).
The roles add no new execution path: they are AgentLoops with restricted registries and role-specific prompts, so M4 safety and M3 parsing apply unchanged inside a collaboration.

The frontend was built by a delegated subagent under a frozen contract; I independently re-ran its verification (tsc, npm test 66, npm run build) and additionally drove the real UI with Playwright against the live backend, which is what exposed the tool-call-id and confirmation-event defects.

Known limits the console shows honestly: memory is read-only (no endpoint to edit it), there is no file-content endpoint (the Files panel shows files_changed and any diffs the stream carried), and there is no PTY (the Terminal tab shows executor commands and results).

M8 was still uncommitted when M9 started (the M8 work tree was never committed by that session), so M8 and M9 are committed together; the M8 file set and the M9 changes cannot be separated by file any more because deps.py, settings.py, api/console.py and api/ws.py carry both.
